html:
A query that finds one user by email takes 2 seconds on a table of 5 million rows. Add one index and it takes 1 millisecond. Indexes are the single biggest performance tool in a database, and also a common cause of slow writes when overused.

The Problem: A Full Scan

SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'ana@example.com';

Without an index, the database reads every row and checks the email: a full table scan. Twice the rows, twice the time. That's O(n).

What an Index Is

An index is a separate, sorted structure that maps values to the rows that have them, like the index at the back of a book. To find "ana@example.com", the database looks in the sorted index instead of reading the whole table.

CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users (email);

How a B-Tree Works

Most indexes are B-trees: a shallow tree where each node holds many sorted keys.

                 [ m ]
           /               \
     [ c   g ]          [ r   w ]
    /   |    \          /   |    \
 [a b][d e f][h..l]  [n..q][s..v][x..z]

To find a value, the database starts at the top and follows one branch per level. Because each node holds hundreds of keys, even a billion rows need only 3 to 4 levels. That's O(log n): a few reads instead of millions.

B-trees also keep keys in order, so they help with:

  • equality: WHERE email = ?
  • ranges: WHERE created_at > '2026-01-01'
  • sorting: ORDER BY created_at
  • prefixes: WHERE name LIKE 'Ana%' (but not LIKE '%ana')

Composite Indexes and Column Order

An index can cover several columns. The order matters, like a phone book sorted by last name, then first name:

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_date ON orders (customer_id, created_at);

This index helps:

  • WHERE customer_id = 42
  • WHERE customer_id = 42 AND created_at > '2026-11-01'
  • WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC

But not WHERE created_at > '2026-11-01' alone, just as a phone book doesn't help you find everyone named "Ana". The rule: put the columns you filter with = first, then the one you filter by range or sort by.

Covering Indexes

If the index holds every column the query needs, the database never reads the table at all:

-- The index has customer_id and created_at, and the query needs only those.
SELECT created_at FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;

That's a covering index, and it's often the fastest a query can get. PostgreSQL also lets you add extra columns just for this with INCLUDE.

Check With EXPLAIN

Never guess whether an index is used. Ask the database:

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'ana@example.com';

Look for "Seq Scan" (a full scan) versus "Index Scan". The plan also shows the estimated and real time of each step.

Why the Index Isn't Used

  • A function on the column: WHERE LOWER(email) = ? can't use an index on email. Create an index on LOWER(email) instead.
  • A leading wildcard: LIKE '%ana' can't use the sorted order.
  • Low selectivity: if a filter matches half the table, like status = 'active', a scan is faster, and the database rightly skips the index.
  • The wrong column order in a composite index.
  • Mismatched types: comparing a text column with a number can prevent index use.

What Indexes Cost

Indexes aren't free:

  • Slower writes: every INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE also updates each index on the table. Ten indexes, ten extra writes.
  • Storage and memory: indexes take space, and they work best when they fit in RAM.

So index the columns your important queries filter, join and sort on, and remove indexes nothing uses. Foreign key columns are a classic missing index: joins and cascading deletes on them get slow without one.

The Answer in Short

  1. Without an index, a lookup reads every row: O(n).
  2. A B-tree index keeps values sorted in a shallow tree: a few reads, O(log n), even for billions of rows.
  3. In a composite index, put equality columns first, then range or sort columns.
  4. Check with EXPLAIN ANALYZE; functions, leading wildcards and low selectivity skip indexes.
  5. Every index slows writes, so index what your queries need, and no more.
